tldr: This paper introduces ART, a framework that equips existing end-to-end VLA models with agentic tool-use reasoning via LoRA to dynamically call external tools (such as image enhancement, object detection, and camera control). By resolving observation noise and ambiguity through tools before generating actions, fine-tuning on just 30K synthetic trajectories improves task success rates by over 20% compared to baselines in challenging, unseen environments like severe darkness and novel viewpoints.
hero_caption: A comparison between conventional VLA models and the proposed ART method. Under dark conditions or ambiguous instructions, standard end-to-end models and CoT-only models (left) fail. In contrast, ART (right) autonomously triggers external tools like low-light enhancement and object detection to improve observations, successfully generating accurate robot actions.
overview:
Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models achieve high manipulation accuracy through end-to-end training on massive datasets. However, this high performance heavily relies on the same conditions seen during training: clean, bright images and pristine initial poses. When exposed to dim lighting, shifted camera angles, or instructions requiring spatial reasoning like "pick the furthest plate," they often fail or freeze. Retraining the entire model to address this incurs immense data collection costs and risks catastrophic forgetting.

To solve this, the authors took inspiration from multimodal agents: instead of forcing the model to solve everything directly, let it autonomously call external tools to clean up its observations before acting. This approach is called ART (Agentic Robot with Tool-use). ART maps tool-invocation triggers to special tokens added at the end of the VLA vocabulary and trains the tool-calling reasoning component using LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation). When generating real robot actions, LoRA is masked out, preserving the original VLA's smooth, dexterous motor capabilities without degradation.

For validation, the authors built the AT Dataset, consisting of 30K tool-use trajectories generated automatically by corrupting existing datasets and adding complex instructions. Evaluated in simulation (LIBERO) and on a 16-DoF dual-arm robot (Astribot S1), baselines dropped below 30% success under perturbed environments. ART, however, achieved dramatically higher success rates of 75% on LIBERO and 62% on the real robot. This demonstrates that reducing action-space complexity through tools yields exceptional generalizability and data efficiency.
contributions: Proposed ART, a framework that dynamically calls external tools for visual enhancement, spatial reasoning, and embodiment adjustments without degrading the manipulation capabilities of end-to-end VLA models.

Designed a two-stage reasoning and training mechanism that activates LoRA only during tool reasoning and masks it during action generation to use the backbone's original weights, preventing catastrophic forgetting.
Constructed a low-cost automated data generation pipeline of 30K trajectories by injecting perturbations into existing robot datasets and using GPT to generate tool-use reasoning processes.

Demonstrated in simulation and on a 16-DoF dual-arm real robot that ART outperforms mainstream baselines by over 20% in task success rates under unseen disturbances such as dim lighting and viewpoint shifts.

sections.heading: Balancing Dexterous Motor Control with Flexible Tool Use
sections.summary: VLA research has split into modular and end-to-end approaches, facing a tradeoff between simplistic motions and vulnerability to unseen environments with catastrophic forgetting. This work unites both paradigms with ART, preserving the high manipulation accuracy of end-to-end models while flexibly invoking external tools.
sections.details:
VLA models for robotics have developed along two main paths. One is the modular approach, represented by works like RoboTool and RoboCodeX. These systems define object recognition and grasping as discrete functions and have language models call APIs. While modularity is clear, they are constrained by predefined discrete functions, making it hard to execute complex tasks that require dexterous continuous control.

The other path is the end-to-end approach, represented by models like OpenVLA and $\pi_0$. These train a single foundation model on massive multitask datasets to output continuous robot control signals directly from images and language. While they deliver precise motions on trained tasks, they are fragile against disturbances such as lighting changes or shifted camera angles. Adapting them to new environments requires expensive additional training. Moreover, because all capabilities are packed into one network, retraining easily triggers catastrophic forgetting of prior skills.

To address the question of whether we can maintain high end-to-end precision while flexibly handling new environmental changes with external tools, the authors developed ART (Agentic Robot with Tool-use). ART constrains and assists the VLA's continuous action space through tool-use, dramatically lowering data dependency while boosting generalizability. This integration is realized through a 30K synthetic tool trajectory pipeline that removes the need for new real-world data collection, paired with a two-stage LoRA fine-tuning method that protects original manipulation skills.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Modular Robotics, VLAs, and LLM Agents
sections.summary: This work sits at the intersection of modular robot action synthesis, end-to-end VLAs, and tool-using multimodal agents. While prior works applied tools to narrow, isolated tasks, ART integrates diverse tools and reasons across entire long-horizon trajectories.
sections.details:
This section reviews the three research areas foundational to ART and clarifies its novelty.

- Modular Robot Action Synthesis: Early approaches like Code as Policies extracted intermediate representations (affordances), such as object positions or segmentation masks, from observations and passed them to predefined control primitives (e.g., `pick_obj` or `place_at_pos`). While swapping tools is straightforward, relying on hand-crafted functions for language-to-action mapping limits complex language understanding and fine motor manipulation.

- Vision-Language-Action Models: Mainstream end-to-end VLAs predict action sequences directly from language, images, and proprioceptive states (such as joint angles). Some methods (e.g., ECoT) incorporate intermediate affordance predictions like bounding boxes to boost reasoning. However, these require large-scale manual affordance annotations and easily break down when input images suffer from noise, darkness, or other visual corruptions.

- Multimodal Agents with Tool-Use: Equipping LLMs and VLMs with web search or image processing tools has advanced rapidly. Recently, models like TIGeR (integrating 3D geometric tools into VLAs) and VLA² (integrating web search) have emerged. Still, these are confined to narrow functions like object grounding or geometric computation. ART takes a significant step forward by combining diverse multimodal tools—visual enhancement, affordance estimation, and embodiment adjustments—into an agentic VLA that autonomously manages them across long-horizon multitask trajectories.

sections.heading: A System Architecture That Injects Tools Without Breaking Motor Control
sections.summary: ART expands the action space to cover language reasoning, tool use, and physical actions, mathematically decoupling observation recovery from action generation. Architecturally, tool states are represented as discrete tokens; LoRA is activated only during tool reasoning and masked during action generation, preventing catastrophic forgetting.
sections.details:
This section covers the mathematical formulation and system architecture of ART.

3.1 Problem Formulation with Tool-Use Reasoning:
Standard VLAs directly predict continuous actions $\boldsymbol{a}_t \in \mathcal{A}$ from clear observations $\boldsymbol{o}_t$. In the real world, however, observations $\tilde{\boldsymbol{o}}_t$ often contain noise and missing details. ART extends the action space to $\mathcal{A}^* = \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{R} \times \mathcal{T}$, where $\mathcal{R}$ denotes natural language reasoning and $\mathcal{T}$ represents discrete tool-invocation actions. The core design philosophy is that accurate physical actions $\boldsymbol{a}_t$ should depend only on the tool-enhanced clean observation $\boldsymbol{o}_t$, rather than raw, corrupted observations $\tilde{\boldsymbol{o}}_t$. This factors the overall optimization objective neatly into two parts: standard VLA action learning and tool-injection learning for reasoning and tool invocation.

3.2 Tool-Injection Architecture:
- Tool Token Injection: For $n$ external tools, binary invocation states are represented as $\boldsymbol{a}_{\mathrm{t},t} \in \{0, 1\}^n$. These discrete choices are mapped to $N$ new tokens appended to the model's vocabulary. This allows standard next-token prediction cross-entropy loss to train tool usage directly.
- Adaptive LoRA Fine-Tuning: The backbone VLA is frozen, and only a LoRA module dedicated to tool reasoning is trained. During inference, the model uses LoRA on the current observation to output reasoning tokens and tool-activation tokens, which execute the chosen tools. When generating physical robot actions from the tool-enhanced observation, LoRA is masked out. This decoupling completely avoids interference with the VLA's pre-trained dexterous action generation.
- Action Chunk Alignment: Modern fast VLAs use action chunking, predicting continuous actions for the next $H$ steps in a single forward pass. ART aligns with this: instead of reasoning about tools at every single control step, tool reasoning runs once every $H$ steps, applying the selected tools' effects to observations across the subsequent $H$ steps efficiently.

3.3 Training Strategy:
The framework builds on the 3B-parameter $\pi_0$-FAST model. Training optimizes two losses: predicting tool-use reasoning tokens (optimizing LoRA parameters $\theta_{\mathrm{L}}$) and autoregressively predicting robot action tokens conditioned on enhanced observations (optimizing backbone parameters $\theta$).

captions.F2: Overall architecture of ART. Given a degraded raw observation (e.g., a dark image), the model outputs a reasoning process and tool tokens via the LoRA module. External tools (visual enhancement, affordance, embodiment) produce an improved observation. The original backbone, with LoRA masked out, then generates the final robot action tokens.

sections.heading: Corrupt and Reconstruct: The Automated Data Pipeline
sections.summary: To avoid expensive robot data collection, the authors automatically expanded existing VLA datasets into 30K tool-use trajectories (the AT Dataset). The pipeline consists of three stages: task perturbation, tool chain selection, and GPT-driven reasoning generation.
sections.details:
Collecting internet-scale robotics data from scratch is extraordinarily difficult. To bypass this, the authors built an automated synthesis pipeline that smartly expands existing manipulation datasets.

4.1 Defining Multimodal Tools:
Tools are categorized into three groups corresponding to the VLA's input modalities (images, language instructions, and proprioceptive states):
- Visual Enhancement Tools: 10 image processing tools including low-light enhancement, denoising, deblurring, and stabilization, handling harsh visual environments.
- Affordance Enhancement Tools: Depth estimation models like Depth Anything and object detectors like DINO-X. For instance, when given a complex spatial instruction like "pick the furthest plate," these tools locate targets and estimate distances precisely.
- Embodiment Enhancement Tools: Adjustments such as rotating or zooming the head camera and resetting the robot arm to an initial pose, correcting for misaligned camera views and bad starting arm configurations.

4.2 Generating Long-Trajectory Tool Reasoning:
Data synthesis runs automatically through three steps:
- Task Generation: Intentional perturbations are injected into existing datasets. These include visual degradations (darkness, noise), affordance demands (altering instructions from "pick the bowl" to "pick the object 30cm in front of the pot"), and embodiment disturbances (shifting camera viewpoints).
- Tool Chain Generation: The system determines the necessary sequence of tools to counteract the injected corruptions (e.g., run the low-light enhancement tool first, then the object detector).
- Trajectory Generation: GPT generates natural language traces explaining why each tool was chosen and how the environment changed after tool execution. Combining these yields 30K long-horizon trajectories of connected reasoning and action steps (the AT Dataset).

captions.F3: Data collection pipeline for ART. (1) Injecting perturbations (visual noise, complex instructions, camera angle shifts) into existing robot data, (2) assigning corresponding tool chains to resolve them, and (3) using GPT to synthesize reasoning traces explaining tool selections.

sections.heading: Conquering Darkness and Shifted Views: Strong Generalization in Sim and Real
sections.summary: Evaluations in the LIBERO simulation and on a 16-DoF dual-arm Astribot S1 robot showed that while SOTA baselines fell below 30% success under disturbances, ART reached 75% in LIBERO and 62% on the real robot, demonstrating that dynamic tool use directly drives robustness.
sections.details:
5.1 Experimental Setup:
Fine-tuning was conducted on the 30K AT Dataset using 8 A800 GPUs for just 1 epoch (batch size 24, initial learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$). Two evaluation environments were used:
- LIBERO (Simulation): Benchmarks systematically injected with lighting changes, noise, ambiguous spatial instructions, and disturbances to initial camera poses and robot configurations.
- Astribot S1 (Real Robot): A 16-DoF dual-arm robot. The FAST baseline was trained on 16K pick-and-place demonstrations covering 80 object types and 10 container types.

5.2 Performance Gains from Tool Integration:
Under generalization tests with perturbations, mainstream state-of-the-art models (OpenVLA and original $\pi_0$-FAST) saw average success rates fall well below 30%, highlighting the fragility of pure end-to-end models against real-world noise and visual corruption.
In contrast, ART achieved an average success rate of 75% in LIBERO and 62% on the real Astribot S1, outperforming baselines by roughly 20% to over 40% depending on the condition. When encountering darkness, ART triggered the low-light enhancement tool to restore visual clarity; when the camera view was offset, it rotated the camera to bring targets back into view, completing tasks reliably.

5.3 Offloading Comparisons and Ablations:
- Comparison with End-to-End Training: Compared against a FAST model fine-tuned on the same amount of data to predict actions directly from raw corrupted inputs without tools, the direct fine-tuning showed negligible improvement. This underscores ART's advantage and confirms the validity of rectifying observations via tools.
- Comparison with Reasoning-Only Model (ECoT): ECoT uses Chain-of-Thought for affordance reasoning. In clean environments, ECoT and ART performed comparably. However, under visual degradations, ECoT's success rate collapsed. Because ECoT cannot repair the corrupted observation, its reasoning process derailed on out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. ART maintained high robustness by fixing the observation with tools before reasoning and acting.

captions.F4: Rollout comparisons during experiments. (a) In dim environments, the baseline FAST (top) loses track in the dark and fails, whereas ART (middle) autonomously invokes the low-light tool to restore visual input and succeeds. (b) In an affordance reasoning task ("put the furthest lemon into the basket"), ART accurately identifies the target location and completes the grasp.

sections.heading: The Next Evolution of Robot Foundation Models
sections.summary: This paper presented ART, uniting end-to-end VLAs with modular tool use. By leveraging 30K synthetic trajectories from existing data and decoupling features with LoRA, the system achieves remarkable robustness and adaptability without catastrophic forgetting.
sections.details:
ART provides an elegant resolution to the ongoing tension between end-to-end manipulation accuracy and modular flexibility in robotics research.

The pipeline of corrupting existing manipulation data to synthesize high-quality reasoning traces dramatically lowers the need for expensive real-world data collection. Furthermore, decoupling tool reasoning from physical control via two-stage LoRA tuning enables plug-and-play capability expansion without sacrificing the manipulation quality of strong base VLA models.

Both simulation and real-robot results strongly suggest that tool use is not merely an auxiliary helper, but a fundamental paradigm for adapting robots to dynamic, noisy real-world environments.

takeaways: Instead of forcing a single neural network to solve everything end-to-end, offloading observation repair and geometric calculations to existing tools dramatically shrinks action-space complexity and data requirements.
When adding agentic capabilities to a VLA, activating LoRA solely for reasoning and masking it during action output prevents catastrophic forgetting of core motor skills.
Injecting perturbations into existing datasets and using GPT to generate tool rationales and reasoning traces offers a highly practical, cost-effective data collection strategy for robotics.
Under visual degradations, reasoning-only (CoT) models break down on out-of-distribution inputs, while models that repair observations with external tools maintain strong robustness.
limitations: Running tool reasoning once every action chunk ($H$ steps) introduces additional inference latency compared to pure end-to-end models.
The system depends on a predefined suite of tools (10 visual enhancement tools, specific detectors, etc.); handling entirely novel perturbations requires designing and adding new tools.
False tool activations (e.g., invoking low-light enhancement when the scene is already bright) risk adding unnecessary visual distortion and processing delays.
